meta.title: Eduversal School Appraisal Framework
meta.description: A five-domain institutional self-appraisal framework for Eduversal partner schools. Aligned with CIS, WASC, NEASC, Danielson-informed practices, and Permendikdasmen No. 21/2025 (Standar Tenaga Kependidikan), replacing Permendiknas No. 13/2007. Schools complete a self-assessment; external evaluators from Eduversal validate and provide commendations and recommendations.

references.name: ACS WASC (Accrediting Commission for Schools) — Focus on Learning
NEASC (New England Association of Schools and Colleges)
Permendikdasmen No. 21/2025 (Standar Tenaga Kependidikan) — principal competency standards, replacing Permendiknas No. 13/2007

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: The expectation is not met. Evidence is absent, invalid, or contradicted by what was observed during the visit. A Needs Intervention Domain Rating requires a mandatory action plan within 4 weeks through the normal improvement process. This is different from Critical Attention, which uses the urgent two-week escalation process.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Practice has started but is inconsistent or partial. Evidence exists but is dated, covers only part of the school, or shows intent more than implementation.

3.label: Strong
3.description: The expectation is met. Practice is established and documented, but monitoring or review is not yet systematic — the school knows what it does, and is beginning to evaluate how well.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The expectation is fully met. Practice is consistent across the school, documented, and supported by a review cycle the school runs itself. Evidence is current and generated by the school's own monitoring rather than assembled for the visit.

meta.rating_scale_provenance_note: On 2026-08-20 the rating-scale labels were aligned to the published Drive instrument 'School Appraisal: Rating Rubric 26-27' per decisions C2/C13: levels 1, 3, and 4 were renamed to Needs Intervention, Strong, and Outstanding (they previously used a different Beginning/Established/Exemplary label set); level 2 (Developing) was unchanged. Level numbers, descriptions, and scoring were not affected.
meta.cycle: The annual cycle runs from Phase 0 to Phase 4, with ongoing support available as needed. Phases 0–3 for every school are completed within Semester 1 (teaching ends 4 December 2026). These phases establish and validate the school quality picture. Phase 4 takes place in May–Jun 2027 and reviews the impact of the two School Development Priorities. Phase 4 does not create a new Domain Rating.
meta.source_document: School Appraisal: Handbook 26-27 + School Appraisal: Overview 26-27

supervision.description: The Visit I Supervisor leads the school's Phase 1 (Teaching Quality) visit, and writes and signs the Annual School Quality Report — the one written report of the cycle, produced after Phase 3. The Visit II Supervisor leads the school's Phase 3 (Validation) visit. Phases 0–2 produce no written report — their findings are shared in person and recorded in the Evidence Guide workbook. Both stay in regular contact with the school throughout the year; each is the designated lead for their own visit, and the Visit I Supervisor is the author and signee of the annual report. Supervisor assignments are fixed at the start of each academic year and published to all partner schools.
supervision.note: "Visit I Supervisor" and "Visit II Supervisor" refer to the PIC (Person in Charge) role within the appraisal process — not to the school's academic level (primary/secondary school). The Visit I Supervisor is the point of contact for that school's Visit 1 and the author and signee of the Annual School Quality Report; the Visit II Supervisor is the point of contact for Visit 2.
responsibilities: Conducting lesson walkthroughs and formative Specialist lesson observations during their respective visit (Visit I at Phase 1, Visit II at Phase 3); these observations do not produce or alter official Teacher Appraisal F2 scores
Monitoring the school appraisal domain progress across the year
Reviewing the two School Development Priorities and their implementation evidence
Maintaining regular communication with the school's Principal and Academic Coordinator
Logging Coordinator Notes in the system at any point during the year
Escalating concerns to the CAO when a school's outcome status shifts to Needs Support or Critical Attention

domain_leads.description: Each of the five domains is led by two experts who own domain quality, calibration and rating consistency across the network. The pair is always split across a school's two visits, so no expert visits the same school twice in a year — full domain coverage comes from the pairing, not from repeat visits.
domain_leads.additional_experts_note: Specialists who hold no domain lead but may join a visit team or cover for a lead. They are selectable in the supervisor and visit-team pickers; they do not own a domain, so they never appear in pairs above.

visit_types.name: Kickoff Session
visit_types.description: Phase 0 launches the self-appraisal cycle. Schools receive the self-evaluation instructions and the School Appraisal: Evidence Guide 26-27 at this session. Before Phase 1, each school must complete or update the Self-Evaluation Summary and working evidence links in the Evidence Guide. A school that has not submitted the required self-evaluation will have its visit rescheduled — the visit cannot proceed without it.

visit_types.name: Teaching Quality Visit
visit_types.led_by: Full team (5 experts, one per domain)
visit_types.description: First on-site visit. Focus: classroom practice, teacher appraisal, curriculum implementation, assessment quality. Includes formal lesson observations, rapid random walkthroughs, student and teacher interviews, and per-domain meetings with school management. Each observation applies two lenses at once — general instructional quality and subject-specific expertise.

visit_types.name: Progress Check-in
visit_types.description: Progress review between the two on-site visits: self-appraisal progress across all five domains, action plan implementation status, and any emerging concerns.

visit_types.name: Validation Visit
visit_types.led_by: Full team (5 experts, one per domain)
visit_types.description: Second on-site visit — leadership, technology and facilities. Validates the school's self-appraisal, cross-references evidence, spot-checks continuity of Phase 1 findings, and produces the Annual School Quality Report.

visit_types.name: Impact Review
visit_types.description: In May–Jun 2027, the school reviews the two School Development Priorities, evidence of change, and what should carry forward. It is developmental only and creates no new Domain Rating. Led by the Visit I Supervisor with an Eduversal representative.

visit_types.name: Follow-up Session
visit_types.led_by: Visit I Supervisor (+ CAO for Critical Attention)
visit_types.description: Targeted support for schools at Needs Support or Critical Attention. Triggered by outcome status or by a Coordinator Note escalation.

visit_types.name: Coordinator Note
visit_types.led_by: Visit I or Visit II Supervisor
visit_types.description: A logged observation or concern. Does not constitute a formal visit.

on_track.label: On Track
on_track.description: The school is progressing as expected. Self-appraisal evidence is developing appropriately, and the action plan is being implemented.

needs_support.label: Needs Support
needs_support.description: Some domains show delay or gaps. The Visit I Supervisor will increase the frequency of check-ins and provide targeted guidance.

critical_attention.label: Critical Attention
critical_attention.description: Significant gaps identified. An urgent intervention plan is required, involving the Visit I Supervisor and Eduversal leadership.

development_rating.description: Development Rating — the banded expression of ONE domain's rating at the end of the appraisal cycle. Each of the five domains carries its own Development Rating and is read on its own terms. It is a development indicator, not a ranking — schools are assessed against the framework standard, not against each other.
development_rating.computed_from: The domain's own rating (1–4), banded. One rating per domain; five ratings per school; no sixth number.
development_rating.distinct_from_outcome_scale: outcome_scale is a per-visit judgment that triggers escalation and follow-up during the year. A Development Rating is the cycle-end position of one domain. A school can be Needs Support at Phase 1 and still finish the year Strong on that domain.
development_rating.label_collision_warning: "Developing" also names an aspect band on the 1–4 rating_scale. Always render this value as a Development Rating with its domain named, so the two cannot be confused — and never as a "School Development Rating", which reads as a whole-school composite.

bands.label: Outstanding
bands.meaning: Strong systems and consistently high-quality practices in this domain. School can serve as a model for the network.

bands.label: Strong
bands.meaning: Effective systems with clear evidence of quality. Minor areas for development that the school is already addressing.

bands.label: Developing
bands.meaning: Several systems in place but require further strengthening. Targeted support is provided by Supervisors and Domain Leads.

bands.label: Needs Intervention
bands.meaning: Significant gaps in this domain. A mandatory action plan is required within 4 weeks through the normal improvement process. Targeted follow-up is provided. If a separate Critical Attention trigger is identified, the urgent two-week escalation process applies instead.

development_rating.no_composite: Eduversal does not publish a single composite school score. The five domains measure different things, and a mean would hide the differences that matter for action. Never average, weight or otherwise combine the five domain ratings into one school score or band. Source: ES 17.8 (docs/research/eduversal/academic-standards/section-17.json) and, in the AY 2026-2027 Academic Services corpus, School Appraisal: Handbook 26-27, School Appraisal: Overview 26-27, School Appraisal: Quick Reference 26-27 and Appraisal Suite: Scorecard Layer 26-27.
development_rating.provenance_note: Until 2026-08-30 this block defined the Development Rating as the mean of the five domain scores, and Central Hub /school-appraisals computed that mean and printed it into the Annual School Quality Report as "School Development Rating: <band> (mean N of 4)". That contradicted ES 17.8 and the school-facing handbook, which already said there is no whole-school composite — so the handbook a school read and the report Eduversal generated for it disagreed. Corrected 2026-08-30 against the AY 2026-2027 Academic Services corpus. The four bands and their meanings are unchanged; they now band one domain at a time.

annual_phases.name: Kickoff
annual_phases.timing: 15 Jul – 27 Aug 2026 (3 weeks before that school's Phase 1)
annual_phases.description: Self-evaluation framework distributed. The Self-Evaluation Summary and evidence links in the School Appraisal: Evidence Guide 26-27 are completed or updated before each on-site visit (Phase 1 and Phase 3) — minimum 5 working days before the visit date; the visit cannot proceed without it.

annual_phases.name: Teaching Quality Visit
annual_phases.description: First on-site round. Two schools visited in parallel each week where they are in different locations; schools in the same city or island are visited consecutively by the same team.

annual_phases.name: Progress Check-in
annual_phases.timing: Sep – Oct 2026 (midpoint between that school's Phase 1 and Phase 3)
annual_phases.description: Led by the Visit I Supervisor. Deadline for all check-ins: 18 Oct 2026.

annual_phases.name: Validation Visit
annual_phases.description: Second on-site round, 55–63 days after that school's Phase 1. Produces the Annual School Quality Report, due within 3 weeks of the visit.

annual_phases.name: Impact Review
annual_phases.description: Closes the improvement cycle. Reviews the two School Development Priorities chosen after the Annual School Quality Report and asks six questions: what did we agree to improve, what was implemented, what changed, what evidence shows impact, what still needs work, what carries forward. Each priority gets an impact status — Achieved, Partly Achieved, Not Yet Achieved, or Carry Forward — recorded in a short Impact Review Record. Phase 4 creates no new Domain Rating, does not reopen the Phase 3 rating, and requires no new evidence pack.

annual_phases.name: Follow-up & Advisory
annual_phases.scope: Schools at Needs Support or Critical Attention
annual_phases.description: Frequency set by outcome status rather than by calendar.

annual_report.name: Annual School Quality Report
annual_report.deadline: Within 3 weeks of the Phase 3 Validation Visit (11 Dec 2026 for AY 2026–2027).
contents: Summary of Phase 1 Teaching Quality Visit findings
Summary of Phase 3 Validation Visit findings
Domain ratings across all five School Appraisal domains (1–4 scale)
Teacher Appraisal aggregate data — school-level, anonymized
EASE Assessment performance summary for the school, with the EASE Growth Version 1 baseline summary as context only (not scored)
EASE Academic participation rate — school-level, anonymized (scores are confidential to the teacher and never reach school appraisal — ES 12.6)
Development Rating for each of the five domains

appeal.window: 10 working days from receipt of the Annual School Quality Report
appeal.note: The decision of the CAO is final.

teacher_appraisal_link.description: The two frameworks remain separate, but they may reuse evidence at the correct level. Individual Teacher Appraisal records never become School Appraisal scores. For Domain 2 (Teaching & Learning Quality), school-owned F2 results may be aggregated into a school-level classroom-practice pattern and considered alongside the wider Domain 2 evidence set in the Evidence Guide: lesson and unit plans, assessment methods, student feedback, professional-development evidence, LMS/technology evidence, and Eduversal's independent formative observations. This reduces duplication while keeping the two scoring systems separate.
teacher_appraisal_link.validation_note: Validation of the school's Framework 2 data. The Eduversal Subject Specialists' own lesson observations during the Phase 1 and Phase 3 visits are not used to score any individual teacher. They are used to test whether the school's aggregated Framework 2 picture matches what a calibrated external team observes in the same classrooms. Where the two align, the school's data is confirmed and the Domain 2 rating follows it. Where they diverge materially, the Domain Lead investigates the reason and triangulates all available Domain 2 evidence before setting the final rating. Eduversal Specialist observations are an external validation source, not a substitute teacher-appraisal score. The report records the size and likely cause of the gap — for example an appraiser-calibration need, an unusual visit week, incomplete school evidence, or a genuine difference in standard. The school's own teacher-level scores are never retrospectively changed by this process; only the school's Domain 2 rating is affected.
teacher_appraisal_link.why_separate_sources: Eduversal Subject Specialists are calibrated against each other through blind-scoring exercises before each visit cycle, and they see one lesson twice a year. The school's appraisers see each teacher six or more times across the year, in the context of that teacher's classes, students and subject. Blending two differently calibrated sources into a single score would make an individual's appraisal less fair, not more — so the appraisal rests on the fuller, closer evidence base, and the external view is used to validate the school rather than to rate the teacher.
teacher_appraisal_link.walkthrough_note: During school visits, Subject Specialists use three coordinated lenses: the Teaching Practice Walkthrough for formative teaching-practice feedback, the Learner Experience Walkthrough for school-level patterns in what students are experiencing, and the School Appraisal Domain lens. Both walkthroughs remain formative. Learner Experience findings do not score individual teachers and contribute to Domain 2 only as aggregated supporting evidence. Walkthrough data contribute to Domain 2 evidence; all five domains are assessed through the complete visit program.

meta.international_alignment: Eduversal Academic Standards Section 24 — School Appraisal Framework: International Alignment. ES 24 is the source of truth for the CIS / ACS WASC FOL / NEASC ACE / Cambridge CSLS / BAN-S-M IASP mappings carried in each domain frameworkAnchors block, and for the four documented scope limits (no Schoolwide Learning Outcomes aspect, no financial or facilities assessment, an annual in-network cycle, and a development rating rather than an accreditation decision). If this file and ES 24 disagree, ES 24 is right and this file needs correcting.

global_benchmarks.description: The frameworks this one is built on. The Eduversal School Appraisal Framework is a deliberate synthesis rather than a copy of any single external model: where these agree, our domains follow them; where they diverge, our domains follow what is defensible in an Indonesian Cambridge school. ES Section 24 holds the full mapping tables and the documented scope limits.
global_benchmarks.authority: Eduversal Academic Standards Section 24 — School Appraisal Framework: International Alignment

items.name: CIS International Accreditation
items.contribution: Nine lettered domains, of which eight apply to Eduversal partner schools — A Purpose and Direction · B Governance, Ownership and Leadership · C Curriculum · D Teaching and Assessing for Learning · E Wellbeing · F Staffing · G Premises, facilities, technology systems and auxiliary services · H Community and Home Partnerships. Domain I (Residential services) covers boarding and homestay and applies to no school in the network. Note that assessment is not a separate CIS domain: it sits inside Domain D. Our five-domain split plus the self-study-then-validation cycle follows the CIS model most closely: mandatory self-study before the visit, an external visiting team, commendations paired with recommendations, an assigned continuity figure, and a formal appeal route.

items.name: ACS WASC — Focus on Learning
items.meta: Accrediting Commission for Schools, WASC · Focus on Learning (K-12)
items.contribution: Four categories — A Organization for Student Learning · B Curriculum, Instruction and Assessment · C Support for Student Personal and Academic Growth · D Resource Management and Development — plus the schoolwide action plan, which is a required deliverable of the self-study rather than a fifth category. Each of our domains answers to one or more of these. WASC's separation of a Focus Visit (instructional quality) from a Full Visit (whole institutional system) is the precedent for splitting our cycle into Phase 1 Teaching Quality and Phase 3 Validation. Note this is the K-12 framework, not WASC Postsecondary.

items.name: NEASC ACE Learning Standards
items.meta: New England Association of Schools and Colleges · 2022 revision
items.contribution: Learning principles plus foundation standards. Pioneered the learner-centred self-evaluation model — schools rate against what students actually experience rather than against compliance checklists. This is why Domain 4 (Student Achievement and Learning Outcomes) exists as a domain in its own right instead of as a sub-section of teaching quality.

items.name: Cambridge School Quality + School Leader Standards
items.meta: Cambridge International · CSLS 2023 (25 standards × 5 areas) + Programme Implementation Guidance 2024
items.contribution: Cambridge's own self-evaluation expectations, plus the 25 School Leader Standards tagged against every domain — visible as the CSLS chips in the domain headers. Tagging them here means a leadership development conversation and a school appraisal rating point at the same standard rather than at two vocabularies.

items.name: BAN-S/M Akreditasi · IASP 2020
items.meta: Badan Akreditasi Nasional Sekolah/Madrasah · Instrumen Akreditasi Satuan Pendidikan
items.contribution: Four components — Mutu Lulusan · Proses Pembelajaran · Mutu Guru · Manajemen Sekolah. Unlike CIS and WASC this is not optional: it is the legal accreditation framework, and partner schools are subject to it whatever their Cambridge status. Every domain carries IASP tags, so evidence assembled for an Eduversal appraisal is substantially what an IASP visit asks for and the Phase 3 Validation Visit can double as an IASP-readiness audit.

items.name: Indonesian competency standards
items.meta: Permendikdasmen No. 21/2025 (Standar Tenaga Kependidikan), which replaced Permendiknas No. 16/2007 (teachers) and No. 13/2007 (principals)
items.contribution: Carried as PMD tags so that staff development and school appraisal cross-walk rather than running as unrelated judgements. Note a known gap, documented in ES 24.6: the PMD chip family resolves against 16/2007 (the four teacher pillars), but D1 and D5 also carry principal competencies from 13/2007, which is not yet in the research archive — those chips render without a verbatim popover, and Kompetensi Supervisi is not tagged anywhere.

live_alignment.note: Aspect titles, expectations and evidence lists follow School Appraisal: Handbook 26-27; per-aspect rating descriptors and the eight Core aspects follow School Appraisal: Rating Rubric 26-27; the four scale descriptors, domain and aspect summaries (first sentence of the Handbook expectation), cycle, visit outcome scale and Teacher Appraisal link follow the Handbook; supervisor note and responsibilities, Development Rating band meanings and Annual School Quality Report contents follow School Appraisal: Overview 26-27. A rating of 1 in a Core aspect triggers a Critical Attention outcome for the whole visit. The School Appraisal: Evidence Guide 26-27 is the scoring document of record.

domains.title: Leadership & Governance
domains.description: This domain evaluates the quality of school leadership, strategic planning, governance structures, legal compliance, and the use of data and evidence in decision-making. Strong leadership provides clear direction, builds institutional culture, and ensures accountability at all levels. It aligns with the CIS Standard on Purpose, Direction & Governance and the NEASC Standard on Governance and Leadership.

frameworks.name: CIS International Accreditation — Domain A (Purpose and direction) + Domain B (Governance, ownership and leadership)
frameworks.edition: Evaluation Framework [Revised]; Quick Guide to Standards, July 2021

aspects.title: Vision, Mission & Strategic Direction
aspects.description: The school has a clearly articulated mission and vision, underpinned by core educational values that are documented and publicly accessible.
expectations: The school has a clearly articulated mission and vision, underpinned by core educational values that are documented and publicly accessible.
The school actively promotes these values across all aspects of school life.
A strategic Plan for Growth & Improvement exists to improve student performance.
Development goals are set through genuine involvement of all stakeholders — parents, students, teachers, and leaders — and communicated clearly through multiple channels.
A feasibility study is conducted for all goals prior to implementation. Goals are SMART and directly address teaching and learning outcomes.
evidence_examples: A1. School development goals document
A2. School Development Plan (P.I.E. model)
A3. Stakeholder consultation records
A4. Published vision and mission statements

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No published vision and mission, or no development plan, or a plan that has not been revisited since it was written. Goals cannot be linked to student outcomes.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Vision and mission exist but are not widely known, or the development plan is a list of intentions without timelines, owners or measures. Consultation was limited to leadership. Goals are general rather than SMART.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Vision, mission and values are documented and publicly accessible. A development plan exists with SMART goals addressing teaching and learning. Stakeholder consultation took place and is recorded. Review happens at year-end rather than during the year.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Vision, mission and values are published and known — staff and students can say what they are without reading them. The Plan for Growth & Improvement is active: goals are SMART, tied to teaching and learning, and reviewed during the year with evidence of what changed. Stakeholders were genuinely consulted, and the school can show how that consultation shaped the goals.

aspects.title: SMART Goals & P.I.E. Model Implementation
aspects.description: Leadership teams are formally assigned for all school development goals, with members who know and can articulate their roles and responsibilities.
expectations: Leadership teams are formally assigned for all school development goals, with members who know and can articulate their roles and responsibilities.
Leadership teams prepare fully based on the P.I.E. model (Plan, Implement, Evaluate).
Goals are monitored through structured action planning with timelines, milestones, and responsible parties. Progress is tracked through documented evidence at regular intervals.
evidence_examples: B1. School Smart Goal documentation
B2. Leadership Team list with assigned goals
B3. Job descriptions for leadership team members
B4. Action plans with timelines and evidence checkpoints

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No assigned teams, or no action plans, or no evidence that any goal has been monitored since it was set.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Teams are assigned but roles are unclear, or action plans exist for some goals only. Progress tracking is irregular or undocumented. The P.I.E. cycle stops after Implement.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Leadership teams are assigned to all goals with written responsibilities. Action plans carry timelines, milestones and named owners. Progress is tracked at regular intervals. The Evaluate step is done but stays descriptive — what happened, not what it means.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every development goal has a named leadership team whose members can explain their role. The P.I.E. cycle is complete: plans are made, implemented, and the Evaluate step produces documented conclusions that change the next plan. Progress checkpoints happen on schedule and are evidenced.

aspects.title: School Leadership Structure & Shared Leadership
aspects.description: An organizational structure facilitates clear, consistent, and transparent communication across all stakeholder groups.
expectations: An organizational structure facilitates clear, consistent, and transparent communication across all stakeholder groups. Effective internal communication processes are in place — regular meetings, clear protocols, and accessible platforms. Roles and responsibilities are clearly defined in written policies and handbooks.

A culture of shared leadership exists, with genuine opportunities for staff to participate in decision-making. Leadership proactively ensures a safe and secure learning environment. Child protection procedures are established and understood by all staff.
evidence_examples: C1. School Organizational Chart (see also Domain 5, Aspect C1)
C2. Staff/Employee Handbook
C3. Parent-Student Handbook
C4. Safeguarding & Child Protection Policy (see also Domain 5, Aspect B1)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No current organisational chart or handbooks, or roles that contradict each other, or no evidence that child protection responsibilities have been communicated to staff.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Structure documents exist but are out of date or do not match practice. Communication is inconsistent between sections or year groups. Shared leadership is stated as a value but staff cannot point to examples.

3.label: Strong
3.description: An organisational chart, staff handbook and parent-student handbook are current and distributed. Roles are defined in writing. Regular meetings and communication protocols exist. Staff have opportunities to contribute to decisions. Child protection procedures are documented and communicated.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The organisational structure is documented and matches how the school actually works. Roles and responsibilities are in written policies and handbooks that staff use. Shared leadership is real: staff can name decisions they influenced. Communication routines are regular and reach everyone. Child protection responsibilities are understood by all staff, not only by the designated lead.

aspects.title: Performance Management & Operational Indicators
aspects.description: Regular and constructive performance evaluation processes support teacher professional growth and accountability.
expectations: Regular and constructive performance evaluation processes support teacher professional growth and accountability.

Approved appraisal records and operational indicators are used to understand principal, leadership-team, and school performance without creating a separate parallel KPI system. Indicators should connect to an approved evidence source, be reviewed as trends rather than isolated numbers, and lead to analysis and follow-up action.

A culture of accountability, peer observation, mentoring, and shared decision-making is cultivated. Ongoing, research-based professional learning is provided with measurable impact on practice and outcomes. Evaluation outcomes are documented and used to inform improvement plans.
evidence_examples: D1. Approved appraisal / operational-indicator records
D2. Evaluation Survey and Report for School Leaders
D3. Most Recent School Annual Report
D4. Professional development plans linked to evaluation outcomes

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No systematic evaluation of teachers or leaders, or no record of staff qualifications, or persistent unfilled posts with no cover arrangement.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Staffing gaps are known but not documented or planned for. Evaluation happens for some staff groups only, or outcomes are recorded but not used. Qualification records are incomplete.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Staffing is adequate and qualifications are recorded. A KPI system evaluates leadership performance. Teacher evaluation happens and is documented. Professional development plans reference evaluation outcomes. Out-of-field teaching is identified but not yet addressed with a plan.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Staffing levels match student numbers and the curriculum offered; vacancies and long absences are tracked with a cover plan that is used. Teachers are qualified for the subject and stage they teach, and any out-of-field teaching has a development or reassignment plan. Performance evaluation runs on schedule for teachers and leaders, and its outcomes visibly shape professional development.

aspects.title: Governance, Compliance & Transparent Decision-Making
aspects.description: Governance is transparent and inclusive, with important decisions informed by stakeholder data.
expectations: Governance is transparent and inclusive, with important decisions informed by stakeholder data. The school adheres to all applicable legal and regulatory requirements. Official government permits, compliance records, and institutional documents are maintained and up to date.
A governing body provides oversight and holds leadership accountable. Governance processes and major decisions are communicated to relevant stakeholders.
evidence_examples: E1. Official government documents (in Edunav)
E2. Institutional operating permits and licenses
E3. Governing body/foundation board meeting minutes
E4. School Academic Calendar (see also Domain 5, Aspect C2)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: Required permits are missing or lapsed, or there is no functioning governing body, or no minutes for the year under review.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Some documents are expired or missing. The governing body meets irregularly, or minutes are thin. Stakeholders learn about decisions after the fact.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Permits, licences and institutional documents are complete and up to date. A governing body meets and keeps minutes. Decisions are communicated to relevant stakeholders. Minutes record decisions but show little discussion or challenge.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: All operating permits and legal documents are current and held in Edunav. The governing body meets on schedule, minutes show genuine oversight and challenge, and major decisions are traceable to stakeholder data. Governance decisions are communicated to those they affect.

aspects.title: Schoolwide Learning Outcomes
aspects.description: The school has defined what every student should know, be able to do, and value by the time they leave — a small set of Schoolwide Learning Outcomes (SLOs) that translate the mission into observable student capabilities.
expectations: The school has defined what every student should know, be able to do, and value by the time they leave — a small set of Schoolwide Learning Outcomes (SLOs) that translate the mission into observable student capabilities. SLOs are known across the community, visible in curriculum and assessment design, and reviewed against evidence of whether students actually achieve them. A concise set of Schoolwide Learning Outcomes is documented, approved by leadership, and derived visibly from the school's mission and values. SLOs describe student capabilities in observable terms, not institutional aspirations — a reader can tell what a student who has met them can do. Students, teachers and parents can name the SLOs and explain what they mean in their own words.

SLOs are mapped into curriculum planning and assessment design across subjects and year groups, not held separately as a statement of values. The school gathers evidence of student attainment against each SLO and reviews it at least annually. SLO review informs the School Development Plan, closing the loop between stated intent and measured outcome.
evidence_examples: Schoolwide Learning Outcomes statement, with its approval record
SLO-to-curriculum mapping across subjects and year groups
Evidence of student attainment against each SLO
Minutes of the annual SLO review and the resulting SDP actions.

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No Schoolwide Learning Outcomes are defined, or a statement exists but is unknown outside leadership. Nothing connects the mission to what students are expected to be able to do.

2.label: Developing
2.description: SLOs are documented and communicated, but are worded as aspirations rather than observable capabilities. They are not yet mapped into curriculum or assessment, and no evidence of student attainment against them is collected.

3.label: Strong
3.description: SLOs are clear, observable, and known across the community. They are mapped into curriculum and assessment design, and the school collects and reviews evidence of student attainment against them annually.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: SLOs demonstrably drive curriculum, assessment and improvement planning. Students can articulate their own progress against them. Review is evidence-rich and feeds the School Development Plan, and the school can show how SLO attainment has changed over time.

domains.title: Teaching & Learning Quality
domains.description: This domain evaluates the quality of classroom practice, lesson planning, assessment methods, feedback quality, evaluation of teaching effectiveness, and the purposeful integration of technology and an LMS in learning. It aligns with the Danielson Framework for Teaching (Domains 1–3) and the CIS Teaching and Learning Standards.

aspects.title: In-Class Documents: Lesson Plans, Observations & Reflections
aspects.description: Teachers produce comprehensive, well-structured lesson and unit plans aligned to curriculum objectives, including clear learning objectives, differentiation strategies, and assessment methods.
expectations: Teachers produce comprehensive, well-structured lesson and unit plans aligned to curriculum objectives, including clear learning objectives, differentiation strategies, and assessment methods.
Detailed classroom observation records are maintained by peers, administrators, and external evaluators.
Teachers engage in regular, thoughtful written reflections on their practice.
Plans reference prior assessment data and demonstrate knowledge of student needs.
evidence_examples: A1. Lesson Plans / Unit Plans
A2. Classroom Observation records
A3. Teacher Reflections
A4. Differentiation strategies in lesson plans

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No lesson planning system, or plans that are not used, or no observation records for the year.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Plans exist for some teachers or some subjects, or plans are templates with little detail. Differentiation is mentioned but not specified. Observations are recorded irregularly. Reflections are brief or missing.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Plans exist for all teachers and contain objectives, differentiation strategies and assessment methods. Observation records are maintained. Teachers write reflections regularly. Plans are sound but generic — they would suit any class of that age.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Lesson and unit plans are complete across the school and aligned to curriculum objectives, with clear learning objectives, differentiation and assessment. Plans reference prior assessment data — you can see the teacher responding to what students did last time. Observation records and written reflections are current, and reflections show teachers changing their practice.

sample_documents.label: A1 Lesson Plans and Unit Plans
Lesson Plan and LMS Observation Log

aspects.title: Assessment Methods
aspects.description: Clear, well-documented assessment policies define grading criteria, frequency, and curriculum alignment.
expectations: Clear, well-documented assessment policies define grading criteria, frequency, and curriculum alignment. A variety of assessment types are used — formative, summative, and diagnostic.
Comprehensive assessment data is collected and analyzed, with trends used to inform instruction.
Well-organized student portfolios are maintained across subjects, demonstrating individual growth over time.
Assessment policies are communicated consistently to students and parents.
evidence_examples: B1. Assessment Policies
B2. Sample Assessments (formative, summative, diagnostic)
B3. Assessment Data and trend analysis
B4. Student Portfolios

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No assessment policy, or no assessment data available for the year, or grading practices that vary between teachers with no agreed criteria.

2.label: Developing
2.description: An assessment policy exists but is out of date or not communicated. Assessment is mostly summative. Data is collected but not analysed. Portfolios are partial or inconsistent between subjects.

3.label: Strong
3.description: A documented assessment policy defines criteria, frequency and curriculum alignment, and has been communicated. A variety of assessment types is used. Data is collected and analysed. Portfolios are maintained. Analysis stops at reporting rather than informing instruction.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The assessment policy is clear, current, and understood by students and parents. Formative, summative and diagnostic assessment are all in use and identifiable in practice. Assessment data is analysed for trends, and you can point to teaching that changed because of it. Portfolios show individual growth over time.

aspects.title: Student Understanding & Goal Setting
aspects.description: Students are actively involved in setting academic and personal goals, with regular teacher check-ins documented.
expectations: Students are actively involved in setting academic and personal goals, with regular teacher check-ins documented. Student-led conferences are held and demonstrate student ownership of learning.
Students can articulate their progress, strengths, and areas for improvement.
Goal-setting documents are maintained and reviewed throughout the year. Students receive specific, constructive feedback that supports their goal progress.
evidence_examples: C1. Goal Setting Documents
C2. Student-Led Conference documentation
C3. Student reflection records and self-assessment forms
C4. Feedback samples on student work

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No student goal-setting process, or no evidence that students are involved in reviewing their own progress.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Goal setting happens in some year groups only, or goals are written once and never revisited. Conferences are teacher-led with students present. Feedback is general.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Goal-setting documents exist for students and are reviewed during the year. Student-led conferences are held and documented. Students receive constructive feedback. Goals are set but the language is the teacher's rather than the student's.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Students set academic and personal goals and can talk about their progress, strengths and next steps in their own words. Teacher check-ins are documented and regular. Student-led conferences show real student ownership. Feedback is specific and connects to the student's goals.

aspects.title: Assessment & Feedback Quality
aspects.description: Constructive, specific feedback is provided to students on assignments and assessments in a timely manner.
expectations: Constructive, specific feedback is provided to students on assignments and assessments in a timely manner. Student, parent, and teacher surveys on assessment and feedback effectiveness are collected and acted upon.
Regular review meetings on assessment and feedback practices are held and documented.
Book scrutiny or work sampling is used to monitor feedback quality across the school. Students have opportunities to respond to and act on feedback received.
evidence_examples: D1. Feedback samples on student work (specific, actionable feedback)
D2. Assessment & Feedback Survey results (student, parent, teacher) with follow-up actions
D3. Assessment & Feedback review meeting minutes
D4. Book scrutiny/work sampling records

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No evidence of feedback beyond marks, or no monitoring of feedback quality at any level.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Feedback is present but mostly grades or brief praise. Book scrutiny happens occasionally. Surveys are collected but results are not shared or acted on.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Feedback samples show specific, constructive comments delivered in reasonable time. Book scrutiny is carried out. Surveys are collected. Review meetings are held and minuted. Follow-up on findings is inconsistent.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Feedback is specific, actionable and timely, and students act on it — improvement is visible in their work. Book scrutiny or work sampling runs on a schedule and findings lead to action. Surveys of students, parents and teachers on feedback quality are collected and followed up. Review meetings produce decisions.

aspects.title: Evaluation of Teaching & Professional Development Records
aspects.description: Comprehensive records of teacher PD participation are maintained, with reflections on impact in the classroom.
expectations: Comprehensive records of teacher PD participation are maintained, with reflections on impact in the classroom.

Internal teacher peer-observation records offering constructive feedback on teaching practices are documented. These are school-owned professional-development records and are separate from Eduversal Network Peer Review.
Individualised teacher improvement plans are developed from evaluation findings.
PD is aligned to school priorities — not ad hoc — and its impact on student outcomes is tracked.
evidence_examples: E1. Professional Development Records
E2. Internal Teacher Peer-Observation / Peer-Feedback Records
E3. Improvement Plans (individualised)
E4. School professional development impact report (see also Domain 3, Aspect F1)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No PD records for the year, or no link between teacher evaluation and any subsequent development activity.

2.label: Developing
2.description: PD records list attendance only. Internal teacher peer observation happens informally without records. Improvement plans exist for some teachers. PD choices are driven by availability rather than need.

3.label: Strong
3.description: PD records are complete with reflections. Internal teacher peer-observation / peer-feedback records exist. Individualized improvement plans are written from evaluation findings. PD is aligned to school priorities. Impact on student outcomes is asserted rather than evidenced.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Professional development is planned against school priorities and individual needs, not chosen ad hoc. Records show participation, reflection on impact, and evidence of changed classroom practice. Internal teacher peer observation is constructive and documented. Individual improvement plans come from evaluation findings and are reviewed.

aspects.title: LMS & Technology Integration in Teaching
aspects.description: Teachers, students, and parents actively use the school's Learning Management System (LMS).
expectations: Teachers, students, and parents actively use the school's Learning Management System (LMS). LMS content is organised, current, and aligned to curriculum standards. Adequate training is provided for all users.

Technology purposefully enhances learning objectives and supports diverse instructional strategies. Innovative practices — flipped classrooms, blended learning, project-based learning — are observed and documented.
Technology is used in both formative and summative assessment with timely feedback.
evidence_examples: F1. LMS analytics and reports
F2. LMS policy and course content documentation
F3. Technology inventory
F4. Training documentation
F5. Lesson plans and materials showing technology integration (see also Domain 3, Aspect G5 — Technology Integration Plans)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No functioning LMS, or no evidence of use by teachers, students or parents during the year.

2.label: Developing
2.description: The LMS exists but is used as a file store, or by some teachers only. Content is out of date. Training was given once at launch. Technology use is occasional and not tied to objectives.

3.label: Strong
3.description: The LMS is in use with organised, current content. Training documentation exists for all user groups. Technology supports teaching and is used in assessment. Usage is uneven between departments.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Teachers, students and parents all use the LMS actively — analytics confirm it. Content is organised, current and aligned to curriculum standards. Technology serves the learning objective rather than decorating it, and innovative practice (flipped, blended, project-based) is visible and documented. Training is provided and refreshed.

domains.title: Curriculum & Academic Programs
domains.description: This domain evaluates the organization and effectiveness of subject departments, the quality of curriculum delivery and professional collaboration, formal observations and walkthroughs, mentoring and peer observation systems, the evaluation of professional development activities, and the integration of cultural contexts and digital policy in curriculum design.

aspects.title: Subject Department Structure & Organization
aspects.description: An updated list of department members is maintained.
expectations: An updated list of department members is maintained. A qualified teacher — preferably with mentorship qualifications — is appointed as Head of Department with clearly defined responsibilities.
Departmental structures facilitate curriculum coherence across year groups.
Department improvement plans are linked to school-wide strategic development goals.
evidence_examples: A1. School subject departments information sheet (members and meeting minutes)
A2. HoD appointment letters and qualification records
A3. Department improvement plans

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No department structure, or no HoDs appointed, or no department planning of any kind.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Some departments lack a designated head, or HoD responsibilities are informal. Improvement plans exist for some departments only, or are disconnected from school priorities.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Department member lists are current. HoDs are appointed with defined responsibilities and appointment letters. Department improvement plans exist and reference school goals. Plans are written but not reviewed during the year.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every department has a current member list and a qualified Head of Department — preferably with mentoring qualifications — whose responsibilities are written and understood. Department improvement plans connect clearly to school strategic goals, and progress against them is reviewed. Structures produce curriculum coherence across year groups, not just administrative order.

sample_documents.label: Sample school subject departments information sheet template

aspects.title: Department Meetings & HoD Coordination
aspects.description: Department meetings are held biweekly, spanning two lessons per meeting.
expectations: Department meetings are held biweekly, spanning two lessons per meeting.
Meeting minutes are recorded and maintained for all departments.
Student outcomes are at the centre of all meeting discussions — including activities to improve teaching, curriculum, assessment, and student support.
HoD coordination meetings led by the principal are held biweekly. Action items from meetings are tracked and followed up.
evidence_examples: B1. Subject department meeting minutes
B2. HoD coordination meeting minutes (principal-led)
B3. Action item tracking logs

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No regular department meetings, or no minutes for the year, or no coordination between departments and school leadership.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Meetings happen but less often than scheduled, or minutes are kept for some departments only. Discussions are operational — timetables, materials, events — rather than about student learning.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Biweekly department meetings are held and minuted. HoD coordination meetings take place. Student outcomes feature in discussions. Action items are recorded. Follow-up on actions is inconsistent.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Department meetings run biweekly across two lessons, with minutes for every department. Student outcomes open the discussion — meetings start with data, not with announcements. Principal-led HoD coordination meetings are biweekly. Action items are tracked and the next meeting revisits them.

aspects.title: Teacher Self-Assessment, Goal Setting & Action Plans
aspects.description: Teachers engage in structured self-assessment using forms that capture strengths, areas for improvement, PD goals, and an action plan.
expectations: Teachers engage in structured self-assessment using forms that capture strengths, areas for improvement, PD goals, and an action plan.
Self-assessments are completed at the start of the year and reviewed. School leaders — principal, AP, HoD — periodically review teachers' yearly goals, self-assessments, and action plans.
Goal-setting is aligned to both personal professional development and school improvement priorities.
evidence_examples: C1. Teachers' self-assessment forms
C2. Goal-setting records with review notes
C3. Teacher action plan templates and completed examples

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No teacher self-assessment process, or forms that were distributed but not returned.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Some teachers complete self-assessments, or forms are collected but not reviewed. Goals are general statements rather than actionable plans.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Self-assessment forms are completed and collected. Goal-setting records exist with review notes. Action plans are written. Leaders review them once, at the start of the year.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every teacher completes a structured self-assessment at the start of the year covering strengths, development areas, PD goals and an action plan. School leaders review these and the review is recorded. Goals connect to both personal development and school priorities. Self-assessments are revisited later in the year.

sample_documents.label: Template and Sample Teacher PD Plan

aspects.title: Formal Observations & Walkthroughs
aspects.description: Formal observations are conducted at least 3 times per semester per teacher by the school's own appraiser team — Subject Leader/Head of Department, Principal, or Academic/Cambridge Coordinator, depending on delegation — and recorded in Edunav Appraisal.
expectations: Formal observations are conducted at least 3 times per semester per teacher by the school's own appraiser team — Subject Leader/Head of Department, Principal, or Academic/Cambridge Coordinator, depending on delegation — and recorded in Edunav Appraisal.
This school-level cycle is the sole source of the official F2 score used in the composite teacher appraisal.

The Eduversal Subject Specialist observation — conducted once per on-site visit, twice a year — is separate and formative: the Specialist gives Glow / Grow / Go feedback directly to the teacher and reports to school leadership, but the observation does not enter any individual teacher's appraisal score.
It is used at school level, as validation evidence for the Domain 2 rating.
Mentors do not conduct formal observations of their mentees to preserve the confidentiality of the mentoring relationship.
Weekly walkthroughs by the principal occur in every classroom and are documented.

Observation records include specific developmental feedback and post-observation conversations are held and recorded. Observation data is used to identify school-wide teaching quality patterns and inform PD priorities.
evidence_examples: D1. Appraisal records in Edunav
D2. Walkthrough observation log (weekly, principal)
D3. Formal observation schedules showing multiple observers
D4. Post-observation feedback records

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No systematic observation cycle, or no records in Edunav for the year, or mentors observing their own mentees.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Observations happen but fall short of three per semester, or cover some teachers only. Walkthroughs are irregular. Feedback is recorded as a rating without developmental comment.

3.label: Strong
3.description: The three-per-semester observation cycle is met and recorded in Edunav. Walkthroughs are logged. Post-observation feedback is documented. Observation data is collected but not analysed for patterns.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Each teacher is formally observed at least three times per semester by the school's own appraiser team, recorded in Edunav. Weekly principal walkthroughs cover every classroom and are logged. Post-observation conversations happen and are recorded with specific developmental feedback. Observation data is analysed for school-wide patterns and shapes PD priorities. Mentors do not observe their own mentees.

aspects.title: Mentoring Programme & Peer Observation System
aspects.description: A mentoring programme pairs experienced teachers with new colleagues — the principal assigns mentors for all first-year teachers.
expectations: A mentoring programme pairs experienced teachers with new colleagues — the principal assigns mentors for all first-year teachers. Mentor-mentee activities are logged throughout the year. Each teacher observes at least one other teacher per month; less experienced teachers do so more frequently.
Peer observation records are maintained and used to support professional dialogue and growth.
evidence_examples: E1. Mentor-mentee list and mentorship activity log
E2. Teachers' peer observation log
E3. Peer observation forms with feedback

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No mentoring program for new teachers, or no peer observation system in operation.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Mentoring is informal or assigned without logging. Peer observation happens occasionally or in some departments only. Forms are completed but carry little feedback.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Mentors are assigned to new teachers and activity is logged. A peer observation system operates with records and feedback forms. The monthly frequency is met for most teachers.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every first-year teacher has an assigned mentor. Mentor–mentee activity is logged through the year and shows a real working relationship. Each teacher observes at least one colleague per month, with less experienced teachers observing more often. Peer observation forms carry feedback that feeds professional dialogue.

aspects.title: Evaluation of Professional Development Activities
aspects.description: All PD activities are evaluated for effectiveness through participant feedback and measurable outcomes.
expectations: All PD activities are evaluated for effectiveness through participant feedback and measurable outcomes. Evaluation data is used to plan future PD programs.
A professional development impact report documents outcomes and improvements.
PD evaluation is tied to teacher growth goals and school improvement priorities. Teachers document how PD learning has been applied in classroom practice.
evidence_examples: F1. School professional development impact report (see also Domain 2, Aspect E4)
F2. PD activity feedback forms and analysis
F3. Teacher application reports linking PD to classroom practice

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No PD evaluation of any kind, or no record of what PD took place.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Feedback is collected for some activities. No impact report, or a report that lists activities rather than outcomes. Application to classroom practice is assumed rather than evidenced.

3.label: Strong
3.description: PD activities are evaluated with feedback forms. An impact report exists. Evaluation is tied to teacher growth goals. Findings are reported but the next PD plan does not visibly reflect them.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every PD activity is evaluated through participant feedback and measurable outcomes. A PD impact report documents what changed. Evaluation findings shape the next PD cycle. Teachers document how PD learning reached their classroom, and that documentation is credible.

sample_documents.label: School professional development impact report template

aspects.title: Cultural & Authentic Contexts and Use of Resources
aspects.description: Curriculum maps incorporate diverse cultural perspectives and authentic learning experiences.
expectations: Curriculum maps incorporate diverse cultural perspectives and authentic learning experiences. Student work demonstrates engagement with culturally diverse content.

Field trips and guest speaker events are documented with objectives, student reflections, and curriculum connections. Up-to-date resource inventories — textbooks, digital tools — are maintained with usage data.
Feedback from students and teachers on resource effectiveness is collected and used.
evidence_examples: G1. Curriculum Maps
G2. Student Work Samples (culturally diverse)
G3. Field Trip and Guest Speaker Logs
G4. Resource Inventories
G5. Technology Integration Plans (see also Domain 2, Aspect F)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No evidence of cultural or authentic contexts in the curriculum, or no resource inventory.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Cultural content appears in some subjects only, or as isolated events rather than planned curriculum. Trip records list logistics without learning objectives. Inventories are out of date.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Curriculum maps incorporate cultural perspectives and authentic learning. Student work samples exist. Trips and speaker events are logged with objectives. Resource inventories are maintained. Feedback is collected but not clearly used.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Curriculum maps show diverse cultural perspectives planned deliberately, not added on. Student work demonstrates genuine engagement with that content. Field trips and guest speakers have documented objectives, curriculum links and student reflections. Resource inventories are current with usage data, and feedback on resource effectiveness leads to decisions.

aspects.title: Digital Policy
aspects.description: The school's digital policy covers guidelines for technology use in teaching, learning, and administration.
expectations: The school's digital policy covers guidelines for technology use in teaching, learning, and administration. The policy is communicated to and understood by teachers, students, and parents.
Programs promoting digital citizenship and ethical technology use are delivered to students. The policy is reviewed regularly to address emerging technologies and evolving risks.
evidence_examples: H1. Digital Policy document
H2. Communication records showing policy distribution
H3. Digital citizenship program documentation
H4. Policy review records with version history

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No digital policy, or a policy that predates the school's current technology and online platforms.

2.label: Developing
2.description: A digital policy exists but is out of date, or has not been communicated beyond staff. Digital citizenship is covered informally. No review history.

3.label: Strong
3.description: A current digital policy exists and covers the required areas. Distribution to all groups is recorded. Digital citizenship programmes are delivered. Review records with version history exist. Reviews are periodic rather than responsive.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The digital policy covers teaching, learning and administration, and staff, students and parents can describe what it requires of them. Digital citizenship programmes are delivered to students and documented. The policy is reviewed on a schedule with version history, and reviews respond to new technologies and risks — including AI use.

aspects.title: Curriculum Design, Coverage & Progression
aspects.description: The documented curriculum defines what students should know and be able to do at each stage, is sequenced to support progression, and offers access and appropriate challenge to all enrolled students.
expectations: The documented curriculum defines what students should know and be able to do at each stage, is sequenced to support progression, and offers access and appropriate challenge to all enrolled students. Coverage against the Cambridge scheme of work (or national curriculum where applicable) is monitored, and gaps are documented with a recovery plan.
evidence_examples: I1. Curriculum map per subject and year group
I2. Vertical sequencing and horizontal articulation records
I3. Coverage tracking against scheme of work + gap recovery plan
I4. Schemes of work showing access and challenge provision

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No documented curriculum beyond a topic list, or no way to show what has been taught against what should have been taught.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Curriculum maps exist for some subjects, or state topics without intended learning. Sequencing is implicit in textbook order rather than designed. Coverage is not tracked, or gaps are known but have no plan. Differentiation appears in intervention records rather than in the curriculum.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Curriculum maps exist for all subjects and year groups. Sequencing is documented. Coverage is tracked and gaps are recorded with a plan. Access and challenge appear in schemes of work. Tracking happens at year-end rather than during the year.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every subject and year group has a curriculum map stating intended knowledge, skills and understanding. Sequencing is deliberate both vertically (year to year) and horizontally (across subjects in the same year), with transition points identified. Coverage against the Cambridge scheme of work — or national curriculum where applicable — is tracked during the year, and gaps have a recovery plan that is followed. Schemes of work show planned access for students who need support and planned challenge for those working beyond expectations.

domains.title: Student Achievement & Learning Outcomes
domains.description: This domain evaluates how well students are learning, how outcomes are tracked and reported, the effectiveness of the Olympiad program and enrichment activities, and how the school supports students with diverse learning needs — including advanced learners, language learners, and students with additional difficulties. It aligns with the WASC Category C criteria for student learning and the NEASC Standard on Student Learning, Programs, and Services.

aspects.title: Student Achievement Data & Dashboards
aspects.description: User-friendly, up-to-date dashboards track student achievement across various metrics.
expectations: User-friendly, up-to-date dashboards track student achievement across various metrics. Regular, detailed progress reports communicate achievement, areas for improvement, and next steps.

In-depth analysis occurs at individual, class, and school levels and is used to set targets and monitor progress. Academic performance data is analyzed at least once per term. Attendance, intervention, and participation patterns may be reviewed alongside achievement data to help explain where learning is improving, stalling, or becoming uneven. Parent and student satisfaction survey results are gathered and used to inform decisions.
evidence_examples: A1. Data Dashboards (student achievement)
A2. Progress Reports (termly, individual)
A3. Data Analysis Reports
A4. Parent and student satisfaction survey results

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No achievement dashboard or data analysis for the year, or reports issued without underlying data.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Dashboards exist but are updated irregularly. Analysis is annual or covers the school level only. Reports give grades without next steps.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Dashboards track achievement and are up to date. Termly progress reports are issued. Data analysis reports exist at all three levels. Surveys are collected. Analysis describes performance without setting targets.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Dashboards are current, usable, and actually used — leaders can show decisions taken from them. Analysis happens at individual, class and school level at least termly, and sets targets that are then monitored. Progress reports tell parents what comes next, not only what happened. Satisfaction survey results feed into decisions.

aspects.title: Olympiad Program: Resources & Academic Follow-Up
aspects.description: The Olympiad Team's aims align with the school's mission and vision.
expectations: The Olympiad Team's aims align with the school's mission and vision. Students are selected through a rigorous, transparent process. Qualified tutors are hired and assigned. A syllabus and study plan are followed regularly.

Regular assessments, including mock exams, are planned, implemented, and followed up. Olympiad student performance is monitored throughout the year with interventions made as needed. All programs are well-documented, and reports are updated regularly.
evidence_examples: B1. Handbook of Olympiad Team
B2. Competition and Achievement list
B3. Student target documentation
B4. Study plan and reading materials/question banks
B5. Tutoring session schedule and attendance
B6. Olympiad student performance report

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No documented Olympiad programme, or a programme with no records of student selection, teaching or results.

2.label: Developing
2.description: The programme runs but selection is informal, or the study plan is not followed, or assessments happen without follow-up. Documentation is partial.

3.label: Strong
3.description: A programme handbook, competition list and student targets exist. Tutors are assigned and sessions are scheduled with attendance records. Study plans and question banks are in use. Assessments happen. Follow-up on results is inconsistent.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The programme's aims are tied to the school's mission. Selection is transparent and documented. Qualified tutors follow a syllabus and study plan. Mock exams and assessments run on schedule, with results triggering intervention for individual students. Performance is monitored through the year and reports are current.

aspects.title: Olympiad Programme: Student Well-being Management
aspects.description: Well-being activities are planned and carried out regularly for Olympiad students in coordination with the relevant school unit.
expectations: Well-being activities are planned and carried out regularly for Olympiad students in coordination with the relevant school unit. Students' personal goals for the Olympiad programme are developed and followed up throughout the year. Well-being goals and career planning are regularly reviewed and documented.
Scholarship students and medal-projected students are followed closely with individualised support.
evidence_examples: C1. Well-being activity schedules and meeting notes with students
C2. Personal goal development records
C3. Refreshment schedule and year-end evaluation report

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No well-being provision for Olympiad students, or no evidence that academic pressure on these students is monitored.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Well-being is addressed informally, or activities are planned but not held. Personal goals exist for some students. No coordination with the school's well-being unit.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Well-being activities are scheduled and meeting notes exist. Personal goal records are kept. A year-end evaluation report is produced. Follow-up during the year is light.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Well-being activities for Olympiad students are planned with the relevant school unit and happen regularly. Each student has personal goals that are developed with them and followed up. Scholarship and medal-projected students receive individualised support that is documented. Well-being and career planning are reviewed on schedule.

aspects.title: Support for Advanced Students
aspects.description: Specific differentiation strategies for advanced students are documented and applied in teaching.
expectations: Specific differentiation strategies for advanced students are documented and applied in teaching. Records of enrichment programmes are maintained — including participation rates, outcomes, and academic impact.
Achievement data for advanced learners is analysed to ensure continued progress and challenge. Teachers demonstrate knowledge of and responsiveness to the needs of advanced learners.
evidence_examples: D1. Differentiation strategies documentation
D2. Enrichment Programme records
D3. Advanced learner tracking and progress data

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No identification of advanced students, or no provision beyond the standard curriculum.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Advanced students are identified but provision is enrichment activities outside lessons only. Tracking is informal. Classroom differentiation is not evidenced.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Differentiation strategies are documented. Enrichment programme records exist with participation data. Advanced learner progress is tracked. Analysis confirms participation rather than impact.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Differentiation strategies for advanced learners are documented and visible in teaching, not only in policy. Enrichment programmes are recorded with participation, outcomes and academic impact. Achievement data for these students is analysed to confirm they are still being stretched. Teachers can describe how they respond to advanced learners.

aspects.title: Language Support for Students
aspects.description: Individualised language support plans are in place for non-native speakers and EAL/ELL students.
expectations: Individualised language support plans are in place for non-native speakers and EAL/ELL students.
Teacher qualifications for supporting language learners are documented.
Regular assessments track language development and academic performance. Language support is integrated with mainstream curriculum delivery.
Student progress in language development is communicated to parents regularly.
evidence_examples: E1. Language Support Plans (individualised)
E2. Teacher Qualifications documentation
E3. Progress monitoring records (language and academic)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No language support provision, or no identification of students needing it.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Language needs are identified but support is generic rather than individualised, or delivered by unqualified staff. Progress is not tracked separately.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Individualised language support plans exist. Teacher qualifications are documented. Progress monitoring records cover language and academic performance. Integration with mainstream curriculum is partial.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Every EAL student has an individualised support plan in use. Staff supporting language learners hold documented qualifications. Assessment tracks both language development and academic performance, and shows progress. Language support is integrated with mainstream lessons rather than delivered only in withdrawal. Parents receive regular updates on language progress.

aspects.title: Identification of Learning Needs & Support for Students with Difficulties
aspects.description: Thorough admissions records capture prior performance, learning needs, and background for each student.
expectations: Thorough admissions records capture prior performance, learning needs, and background for each student.
Comprehensive documentation of special education needs exists — including IEPs, accommodation strategies, and support plans.

Detailed logs record interventions, accommodations, and their effectiveness. Specialist reports from psychologists and speech therapists inform individual support strategies. Feedback from students and parents on support effectiveness is collected and used to improve provision.
evidence_examples: F1. Admissions records
F2. Special Education Needs documentation (IEPs, accommodation strategies)
F3. Student Support Logs (interventions, effectiveness)
F4. Specialist reports (psychologist, speech therapist)
F5. Student and parent feedback on support effectiveness

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No systematic identification of learning needs, or no support documentation for students known to have difficulties.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Needs are identified at admission but documentation is incomplete, or IEPs exist without evidence of classroom implementation. Intervention logs are partial.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Admissions records are complete. SEN documentation including IEPs exists. Support logs record interventions. Specialist reports are held where relevant. Effectiveness is recorded but not reviewed.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Admissions records capture prior performance, learning needs and background for every student, and are used. IEPs and accommodation strategies are current and implemented — teachers know what they say. Support logs record interventions and their effectiveness. Specialist reports inform strategy. Student and parent feedback on support quality is collected and improves provision.

domains.title: School Culture & Community
domains.description: This domain evaluates the quality of the school's culture and climate, the effectiveness of internal communication and organizational management, safeguarding and child protection, parent and community engagement, educational programs and co-curricular activities, and staff well-being. It aligns with the NEASC Standard on School Culture and Community Engagement and the KHDA framework for safeguarding, health, and well-being.
