aspects.title: School Culture, Climate & Student Behaviour
aspects.description: Students demonstrate behaviours consistent with the school's mission and values in daily school life.
expectations: Students demonstrate behaviours consistent with the school's mission and values in daily school life.

A positive, respectful, and inclusive culture is observable across all settings. Clear behaviour management policies are in place, communicated, and consistently enforced. Behaviour data is tracked and used to identify patterns and inform interventions. Where appropriate, schools review incident frequency, recurrence, resolution time, participation in behaviour-support/restorative processes, and student/staff perceptions of safety to understand whether interventions are working.
A culture of mutual respect among students, staff, and parents is actively cultivated.
evidence_examples: A1. Behaviour Management System documentation
A2. Parent-Student Handbook (conduct section)
A3. Behaviour incident data and trend analysis
A4. Student and parent satisfaction survey results (culture section)

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No behaviour policy in use, or no record of behaviour incidents, or a culture that visibly contradicts the school's stated values.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Behaviour policy exists but enforcement is inconsistent, or incident data is recorded without analysis. Survey results are collected but not shared.

3.label: Strong
3.description: A behaviour management system is documented and communicated through the parent-student handbook. Behaviour incidents are recorded and analysed for trends. Satisfaction surveys are collected. Application of policy varies between staff.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Student behaviour reflects the school's stated values in daily life, and this is observable in corridors and classrooms, not only in policy. Behaviour policies are clear, communicated and applied consistently by all staff. Behaviour data is tracked, patterns are identified, and interventions follow. Survey results confirm students and parents experience the culture the school describes.

aspects.title: Safeguarding & Child Protection
aspects.description: Robust child protection safeguards are in place — including background checks, mandatory training, and a clear code of conduct for all staff.
expectations: Robust child protection safeguards are in place — including background checks, mandatory training, and a clear code of conduct for all staff. A Safeguarding and Child Protection Policy is current and reviewed annually.
All staff receive safeguarding training on induction and annually thereafter. Clear reporting and escalation procedures are documented and understood by all staff.
Site security, visitor management, and online safety protocols are implemented.
Emergency and crisis management procedures are documented and regularly practised.
evidence_examples: B1. Safeguarding & Child Protection Policy (see also Domain 1, Aspect C4)
B2. Emergency / Crisis Manual
B3. Staff safeguarding training attendance records
B4. Reporting and escalation procedure documentation

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No current safeguarding policy, or missing background checks for staff in contact with students, or no safeguarding training in the year, or no reporting procedure.

2.label: Developing
2.description: A policy exists but is more than a year old, or training is delivered to some staff only, or background check records have gaps. Reporting procedures are written but staff are unsure of them. Drills are recorded but irregular.

3.label: Strong
3.description: A current policy exists and has been reviewed within the year. Background checks are documented for all staff. Training attendance records are complete. Reporting and escalation procedures are documented and communicated. An emergency manual exists and drills have taken place.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The Safeguarding and Child Protection Policy is current, reviewed annually, and staff can describe their responsibilities under it. Background checks are complete for all staff and volunteers. Safeguarding training is delivered at induction and annually, with attendance tracked. Reporting and escalation routes are known — staff can say who to tell and how. Site security, visitor management and online safety are in place. Emergency procedures are practised, not only written. Records are reviewed for patterns.

aspects.title: Communication Structures & Organisational Management
aspects.description: An organisational structure facilitates clear, consistent, and transparent communication at all levels.
expectations: An organisational structure facilitates clear, consistent, and transparent communication at all levels.
Effective internal communication processes are in place — regular meetings, protocols, and accessible digital platforms. External communication to parents is regular, clear, and multi-channel.
A School Academic Calendar is maintained, communicated, and followed. All stakeholders can access relevant information through clear and accessible channels.
evidence_examples: C1. School Organizational Chart (see also Domain 1, Aspect C1)
C2. School Academic Calendar (see also Domain 1, Aspect E4)
C3. Internal communication platform evidence
C4. Parent communication samples

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No functioning internal communication structure, or no published academic calendar, or parents who cannot access basic school information.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Communication depends on individuals rather than systems. The calendar is published but changes are not communicated. Some stakeholder groups are consistently missed.

3.label: Strong
3.description: An organisational chart and academic calendar are current and distributed. Internal communication platforms are in use. Parent communication samples show regular contact. Communication reaches most groups but some sections are less well served.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: The organisational structure supports clear communication at every level and matches practice. Internal communication routines — meetings, protocols, digital platforms — are used consistently and reach all staff. Parent communication is regular, clear and multi-channel. The academic calendar is published, followed, and changes are communicated promptly.

aspects.title: Educational Programmes & Co-Curricular Activities
aspects.description: Leadership promotes high-quality educational programmes accessible to all students.
expectations: Leadership promotes high-quality educational programmes accessible to all students. Individual student growth through programmes is tracked and reported.

A range of co-curricular activities — academic, creative, sporting, cultural, and service — is offered. Student participation is tracked and programmes are reviewed annually for relevance, quality, and impact. Reviews may draw on participation trends, attendance, student feedback, planned-event completion, achievement or recognition, and curriculum/learning connections where relevant.
evidence_examples: D1. Curriculum Documentation for all educational programmes
D2. Co-curricular programme calendar and activity list
D3. Student participation and achievement data
D4. Programme review records

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No co-curricular provision, or no record of what programmes ran during the year.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Co-curricular activities are offered but the range is narrow, or participation is not tracked, or access depends on cost or selection. Review is informal.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Programme documentation and a co-curricular calendar exist. Participation and achievement data are collected. Programmes are reviewed annually. Review confirms delivery rather than examining impact.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Educational programmes are documented and genuinely accessible to all students — participation data confirms it, including for students who need support. A broad co-curricular range covers academic, creative, sporting, cultural and service activities. Individual student growth through programmes is tracked. Annual review examines relevance, quality and impact, and changes follow.

aspects.title: Parent & Community Engagement
aspects.description: The school communicates regularly with parents through multiple channels — newsletters, app, parent portal, and meetings.
expectations: The school communicates regularly with parents through multiple channels — newsletters, app, parent portal, and meetings. Parent-teacher conferences are held at least twice per year and are structured and productive.

A parent satisfaction survey is conducted annually, and results inform school actions. A formal parent representative body (POMG or school committee) has a clear and active role. Community partnerships are in place and linked to student learning.
evidence_examples: E1. Parent communication samples
E2. Parent-teacher conference schedule and records
E3. Parent satisfaction survey results and follow-up actions
E4. POMG / parent committee meeting minutes
E5. Community partnership documentation

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No structured parent communication, or no parent-teacher conferences during the year, or no parent representative body.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Communication is one-way and irregular. Conferences happen once a year or are poorly attended. Survey results are collected but no actions follow. The parent body meets rarely.

3.label: Strong
3.description: Parent communication samples show regular multi-channel contact. Conferences are held twice a year with records. The parent survey is conducted annually with follow-up actions recorded. POMG or committee minutes exist. Partnerships are documented.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Parents hear from the school regularly through several channels and say communication is clear. Parent-teacher conferences happen at least twice a year and are structured around student progress. The annual parent survey produces actions that are communicated back to parents. The parent representative body has a real role in school life. Community partnerships connect to student learning.

aspects.title: Staff Well-being & Professional Climate
aspects.description: Staff well-being is actively monitored through annual surveys and informal check-ins.
expectations: Staff well-being is actively monitored through annual surveys and informal check-ins. Workload management ensures sustainability — realistic meeting schedules, clear marking policies, and manageable expectations.
A culture of recognition acknowledges staff contributions formally and informally. Staff turnover is monitored and linked to satisfaction data and retention strategies.
Staff are involved in decisions affecting their professional lives and feel their voices are heard.
evidence_examples: F1. Staff well-being survey results and follow-up report
F2. Staff/Employee Handbook (work conditions and support)
F3. Staff recognition records
F4. Staff turnover data and exit interview insights

1.label: Needs Intervention
1.description: No well-being monitoring, or turnover that is high and unexamined, or staff with no channel to raise concerns.

2.label: Developing
2.description: Well-being is discussed but not measured, or a survey is run without follow-up. Workload concerns are known but unaddressed. Recognition is occasional. Turnover is not analysed.

3.label: Strong
3.description: A staff well-being survey is conducted with a follow-up report. The staff handbook covers working conditions and support. Recognition records exist. Turnover data is collected with exit interview insights. Actions from survey findings are planned but not yet completed.

4.label: Outstanding
4.description: Staff well-being is monitored through an annual survey and regular informal check-ins, and results lead to visible changes. Workload is actively managed — meeting schedules, marking policy and expectations are realistic and reviewed. Recognition of staff contribution is both formal and everyday. Turnover is monitored against satisfaction data, and exit interviews inform retention. Staff can name decisions they influenced.
